The last two weeks I was a bit immersed in the European and Middle Power AI discourse. One thing that could help: get clearer on what objectives address which consequences by actually naming your worries.

A weak European position across the AI stack could lead to severe consequences. How severe depends on AI's future capabilities. Here's a categorization attempt:

- Prosperity. Europe might still grow richer in absolute terms, but its relative income declines. The wealth AI creates accrues along the tech stack whose high-margin parts are outside Europe.

- Access. Frontier capability reaches European governments and companies late or not at all. Staged release becomes the default, anti-distillation measures limit access, compute scarcity means providers prioritize, or access becomes a bargaining chip in trade negotiations.

- Agency. Europe's enforcement power degrades as its market matters less to AI companies. It steers AI development less, knows less about frontier systems, and loses the ability to set and enforce its own rules.

- Security. Europe defends itself with AI models hosted by others. If frontier AI becomes a national security capability, Europe uses it on conditions set abroad—and access could be restricted at any point.

- Strategic relevance. A Europe that grows more slowly, defends itself less well, and decides less becomes less geopolitically relevant. Alliances rely more on goodwill than strategic mutual dependence.

- Catastrophe. AI development could lead to catastrophe through cyber, biology, or loss of control. Europe bears the consequences despite not causing them.

Most of these consequences require no hostile intent toward Europe. Compute scarcity, staged releases driven by security considerations, slower adoption, and race dynamics can lead to them on competitive economic terms or US national security grounds.

I recently spent some time thinking about what Europe should do regarding AI. Others have spent much more time, including this great strategy. I agree with a lot of it, but I put somewhat more weight on two things:

1. Partner with the US as the mainline strategy.
2. Europe's biggest economic opportunity may be in complements to frontier AI (not substituting): robotics, advanced manufacturing, pharma, biotech. Leverage existing strengths and ask what becomes dramatically more valuable if frontier AI exists?

More generally, a lot of AI strategy isn't really AI-specific. It's the familiar required reform agenda covering labor markets, capital markets, etc. All made considerably more urgent by AI.

Today I’m launching the Center for Technology & Statecraft (CTS), an initiative inspired by the lessons I learned first as a policy researcher and later in the White House.

I'm an optimist about technology. Institutions adapt to disruptions — whether the industrial revolution, computing, the internet — through competition, self-correction, and iteration, and we mostly figure it out in the long run.

But we've never had to adapt to a technology that is both this transformative and developing this fast. AI capabilities continue to scale rapidly with no sign of slowing, and it's a full-time job just to keep up with model releases. I worry policy will stay reactive right up until we face immense disruptions — including basic challenges to human agency and relevance in a world of powerful AI.

Even still, I believe policy can steer this transition, but only with foresight and the right information.

CTS aims to provide just that. Our two initial policy focus areas:

1) How policy can shape virtual and physical automation over the next decade as we reimagine the social contract in light of advanced AI.

2) How to manage long-term strategic US-China AI competition while ensuring stability.

These focus areas will build on a deep model of the AI value chain, from chipmaking tools, to the compute, algorithms, and data that make AI, to the tokens, agents and robots that affect the world.

For more on our worldview and research philosophy, read https://t.co/yD25oZWBb4.

I’ve seen firsthand how technical, forward-looking research can inform policy if it’s ready for the policy window. After a decade as an IP and tech lawyer, I joined a think tank, CSET, in 2019 to study AI chips, their supply chains, and AI policy. This was three years before ChatGPT, so these weren't seen as urgent topics at the time.

Soon after, AI quickly became an increasingly salient policy issue. From 2021–2025 I served in the White House NSC and the Commerce Department and put new policy ideas into practice (alongside many brilliant colleagues).

One goal of CTS is to scale this kind of experience to a whole team: @KonstantinPilz @nchlsbrwn @amelia__michael @mary_clare_m already bring a wealth of technical and policy expertise and we’ll continue to grow to tackle an ambitious research agenda.

We're thrilled to be supported by and affiliated with @IFP, and grateful to the advisors and colleagues who helped get CTS off the ground, including @ohlennart, @fiiiiiist, @AlecStapp, and @calebwatney.

Our first major reports will launch soon. You can follow us at @techstatecraft.

quoted.text:
Lots of effort goes into working out what AI models can do. Much less into what those capabilities actually imply about risk.

Two new @GovAIOrg reports do some of the deepest such work out there, focused on cyber. 

First, AI-enabled worms, software that spreads between computers and destroys encrypts data, in a report by John Halstead and @lucafrighetti. The bottleneck is "elite exploits": ones that spread with no user interaction, run code with high privileges, and work against widely used software. If frontier AI let a quarter of moderately skilled actors build those, expert and forecaster estimates put marginal damages in the tens of billions a year, and roughly triple the odds of a single >$10B worm.

How do we know elite exploits are a major limiter? In 2017, there was there was a major leak from the NSA, which included some really powerful zero days. Within months of that, two of the most damaging cyberattacks ever occurred – WannaCry and NotPetya – and both of them used Eternal Blue, which was included in the leak. These attacks caused around $10B in damages, but with some minor tweaks could have got up to 100B. WannaCry for example, included an off-switch, and was deactivated less than a day after being released. 

Matt van der Merwe asks what a $100B attack on the US grid would take. (That $100B threshold is what OpenAI says they'll focus on in their Prepardness Framework.) Answer: blacking out 100M people for about a week, which is four orders of magnitude beyond any grid cyberattack on record. There's no single technical bottleneck – the binding constraint is the operational capacity to coordinate attacks on dozens to hundreds of targets at once.

Which makes $100B a bad threshold to hang mitigations on. Models that could get lower-skilled actors there would already be more dangerous elsewhere, and top-tier states plausibly have the capacity already – what stops them is fear of retaliation, not skill. $10B attacks look qualitatively easier, and are probably the more useful trigger.

CoAsia’s revenue is spiking again. The last time it spiked like this, @SemiAnalysis_ reported the channel was being used to route export-controlled Samsung HBM into China (Jan–Mar 2025).

CoAsia distributes Samsung memory and other products. Their largest segment is "Hong Kong Group"—Greater China is their main market. CoAsia is Samsung's sole HBM distributor for Greater China. They've been Samsung's official foundry agent for the Chinese region for years.

On Dec 2, 2024, the US announced new export controls on HBM to China with a Dec 31 compliance date.

The surge began in January. In Jan 2025, revenue jumped to 4.87B TWD. Feb 4.79B, Mar 4.86B. Roughly 2x the 2024 baseline. Right after the HBM rules took effect.

On Apr 16, 2025, @SemiAnalysis_ published an analysis describing how Samsung HBM was allegedly being routed from CoAsia to Faraday (ASIC design) to SPIL (packager), then diverted to China.

This revenue surge later collapsed, probably because someone looked into this and stopped it. Down ~67% from peak within weeks of the SemiAnalysis piece.

Now, in March 2026, revenue jumped to 4.63B TWD—basically the same magnitude as the first surge.

This could be an upswing given the current memory shortage. But if I wanted to build AI chips—which Chinese designers desperately want to do—I'd be doing everything I could to get my hands on HBM. 
Worth looking into.

quoted.text:
Some thoughts on the open weights debate. Most concerns I hear are based on misconceptions, and the actually worrying things barely come up. Genuinely keen to hear pushback.

Not debating the ecosystem and economic benefits of open weights here, same as for open-source software (related but different debate). Mostly on the US-China open weights angle.

A few things I think are misunderstood:
1. A common view is that China gets access to data or makes money. Roughly backwards for open models. The whole point is you download and run it on your own hardware. No revenue flows back, no data flows back. 
If anything, open weights reduce your exposure to the releaser, not increase it. Closed hosted APIs (like using DeepSeek on DeepSeek's site) are where data actually moves.

2. Are models actually that sticky? People swap them weekly, often with a couple lines of code. The brand and ecosystem case for the releaser is thinner than claimed.

Risks I do see, but that get less airtime:
1. Sleeper-agent-style behaviour baked into weights you can't audit. A model could look fine in normal use, then trigger on a specific input and write insecure code or exfiltrate data. Gets worse with more autonomy.

2. Same with embedded values. Imagine education systems globally running on weights with someone else's framing of history.

3. License creep. Free initially, fees later once you cross some (user) threshold (Llama-style).

4. Stack lock-in (but same goes with closed ones). Selling you the model, the hardware, and the phone preloaded with it (then the data might flow back to a specific API in a specific country).

But notably, I think most of these risks are low right now, or don't exist yet (licenses, stack lock-in). And, as said, IMO models aren't sticky.

I think open releases are just a strong counter-strategy. If you can't capture API revenue at the closed frontier, open releases let you leverage US compute (to the degree it gets deployed there) and eat up the discourse.

Personally, the sleeper-agent worry might be enough to tip the balance for me, which is why I'd want strong open models that are truth-seeking and ideologically neutral. (And that's why I'd take US models over the alternatives.) But that's not what I'm hearing in the debate, and instead lots of confusion around open source vs open weights.

quoted.author: anton_d_leicht
quoted.text:
Most countries won't do what it takes to build their own frontier AI. But they don't want to be dependent on foreign AI without a backup. 

@SamWinterLevy and I argue there's a middle path: AI middle powers could retain 'AI Breakout Capacity'. 

There's precedent: Japan doesn't have a nuclear weapon, but always retains the capacity to build one on short notice.

Middle powers can make strategic choices today to ensure their ability to build frontier systems tomorrow: onshore compute, secure chip purchasing rights, sustain pre-training expertise, and create the right legal basis and private-sector vehicles for a sprint.

They'd still have to spend big to build frontier systems later on. But the longer they retain breakout capacity, the longer they can afford to wait: to see if interdependence with America can work, or until their electorate will let them go all-in on an AI moonshot. 

Until then, the middle path is their wisest choice: hope that U.S. alignment works out, but retain the capacity to deal with being cut off for good. 

Read more in our latest for @CarnegieEndow's @CEIPTechProgram:  https://t.co/FWYgzMgbPm

Some additional personal comments: I'll miss some of the on-the-ground policy work, but many of the pathways to influence are mostly closed (might share more on this later). Nonetheless, I'll keep tracking AI chips, export controls, China's AI compute ecosystem, and policy work closely. There will soon be a new crew with some of the best folks I know focusing on this.

I think I'm best at starting with something weird and conceptual, then making it happen. That's what worked with AI & Compute: started with tracking its relevance (Epoch AI), figured out how it could be used for policy (GovAI), then moved to DC to make policy happen. I had a blast.

This bet is similar: weird, maybe a bit too early, but the curve might go up just as steep. Hopefully it leads to similar fruits.

Now, on the Foundation itself. The OpenAI Foundation (where I now work) is not the OpenAI PBC that’s building the AI models. We’re like a dozen folks. Foundation employees hold no equity. I remain a proud member of—what some call—the permanent underclass.

But seriously, people have healthy skepticism about the Foundation, and rightly so. It has made big promises. I hope we deliver on them, including when it comes at a cost to the AI industry but to the benefit of humanity.
